apmo-2020-01.title: Directed angles
apmo-2020-01.body:
We use directed angles between lines, modulo $180^\circ$.

**Step 1: $CA=CB$.** Since $DE\parallel BA$, then since $B,D,F,E$ are concyclic, $E$ lies on line $FC$, and $A,B,C,F$ lie on $\Gamma$:
$$\angle(BA,BC)=\angle(DE,DB)=\angle(FE,FB)=\angle(FC,FB)=\angle(AC,AB).$$
If triangle $ABC$ is labelled counterclockwise, $\angle(BA,BC)\equiv-\angle B$ and $\angle(AC,AB)\equiv-\angle A \pmod{180^\circ}$, so $\angle A=\angle B$ (both lie in $(0^\circ,180^\circ)$). Hence $CA=CB$, and in directed form
$$\angle(BA,BC)=\angle(AC,AB).\tag{1}$$

**Step 2: $A,P,F,E$ are concyclic,** where $P=AC\cap BF$. By the tangent–chord angle at $A$, then (1), then $\Gamma$, and since $E$ lies on line $FC$:
$$\angle(AE,AP)=\angle(AE,AC)=\angle(BA,BC)=\angle(AC,AB)=\angle(FC,FB)=\angle(FE,FP).$$
So $\angle(AE,AP)=\angle(FE,FP)$ and $A,F,E,P$ are concyclic.

**Step 3: $EP\parallel AB$.** In circle $APFE$, then by the tangent–chord angle at $A$ (chord $AF$):
$$\angle(PE,PF)=\angle(AE,AF)=\angle(BA,BF).$$
Since $PF$ and $BF$ are the same line, $PE\parallel BA$.

So $P$ lies on the line through $E$ parallel to $AB$, which is line $DE$. Thus $P$ lies on $AC$, $BF$ and $DE$: the three lines are concurrent. ∎

apmo-2020-01.title: Radical centre
apmo-2020-01.body:
Let $P=BF\cap DE$. By the tangent–chord angle, $\angle(EA,AB)=\angle(CA,CB)$, and as $ED\parallel AB$, $\angle(EA,ED)=\angle(CA,CD)$: so $A,D,C,E$ are concyclic.

Then $\angle(FA,FP)=\angle(FA,FB)=\angle(CA,CB)=\angle(CA,CD)=\angle(EA,ED)=\angle(EA,EP)$, so $A,P,F,E$ are concyclic. Also $\angle(PE,PA)=\angle(FE,FA)=\angle(FC,FA)=\angle(BC,BA)=\angle(BD,BA)$, and since $PE$ is line $DE$, i.e. $\angle(PD,PA)=\angle(BD,BA)$, the points $A,B,D,P$ are concyclic.

Now consider the three circles $(BDFE)$, $(APFE)$, $(BDPA)$. Their pairwise radical axes are $EF$, $AP$, $BD$, which therefore concur. But $EF\cap BD=C$ (line $EF$ is line $CE$, line $BD$ is line $BC$). Hence $C$ lies on $AP$, i.e. $P$ lies on $AC$. So $AC$, $BF$, $DE$ all pass through $P$. ∎

apmo-2020-02.title: Counterexample above 2, two observations at 2
apmo-2020-02.body:
**$r>2$ fails.** Choose a positive integer $a\ge\frac1{r-2}$ and put $a_n=a+\lfloor n/2\rfloor$. Then $a_{n+2}=a_n+1\ge a_n$, and since $a_{n+1}\ge a_n\ge a$,
$$a_n^2+ra_{n+1}\ge a_n^2+2a_n+(r-2)a_n\ge a_n^2+2a_n+(r-2)a\ge a_n^2+2a_n+1=a_{n+2}^2 .$$
So the inequalities hold, but $a_{n+2}>a_n$ for all $n$.

**$r=2$ works.** Let $(a_n)$ satisfy the inequalities with $r=2$.

* (a) If $a_{n+1}\le a_n$, then $a_{n+2}^2\le a_n^2+2a_{n+1}\le a_n^2+2a_n<(a_n+1)^2$, so $a_{n+2}\le a_n$, hence $a_{n+2}=a_n$.
* (b) If $a_n\le a_{n+1}$, then $a_{n+2}^2\le a_{n+1}^2+2a_{n+1}<(a_{n+1}+1)^2$, so $a_{n+2}\le a_{n+1}$.

There is an index $N$ with $a_{N+1}\le a_N$: take $N=1$ if $a_2\le a_1$; otherwise (b) with $n=1$ gives $a_3\le a_2$, take $N=2$.

**Claim.** For all $j\ge0$: $a_{N+2j}=a_N$ and $a_{N+2j+1}\le a_N$. For $j=0$ this is the choice of $N$. If it holds for $j$, then $a_{N+2j+1}\le a_{N+2j}$, so (a) gives $a_{N+2j+2}=a_{N+2j}=a_N$. Now $a_{N+2j+1}\le a_{N+2j+2}$, so (b) gives $a_{N+2j+3}\le a_{N+2j+2}=a_N$.

The terms $a_{N+1},a_{N+3},a_{N+5},\dots$ are non-decreasing (as $a_{n+2}\ge a_n$ always) positive integers bounded by $a_N$, so they are constant from some $a_{N+2J+1}$ on. With $M=N+2J$, both $a_{M},a_{M+2},\dots$ and $a_{M+1},a_{M+3},\dots$ are constant, i.e. $a_{n+2}=a_n$ for all $n\ge M$.

Finally, any $r<2$ also satisfies the condition (its hypothesis is stronger), so $r=2$ is the largest such number. ∎

apmo-2020-03.title: Eventually a doubling chain
apmo-2020-03.body:
For a finite set $T$ let $s(T)$ be the sum of its elements ($s(\varnothing)=0$). A *representation* of $n$ is a finite subset of $S$ with sum $n$.

**$k=2^a$ works.** Let $A=\{1,2,4,8,\dots\}$, let $B'$ be any $a$ positive integers that are not powers of $2$, $S=A\cup B'$, and $m=\max(1,s(B'))$. For $n>m$ and any $B''\subseteq B'$, $n-s(B'')>0$ has exactly one binary representation, i.e. exactly one representation by elements of $A$. Every representation of $n$ consists of its part $B''$ in $B'$ and a binary representation of $n-s(B'')$, so $n$ has exactly $2^a$ representations.

**Necessity.** Suppose $S$, $m$ work for $k$. Enlarging $m$ keeps the property, so assume $m\ge2$. $S$ is infinite (a finite set has finitely many subset sums). Note: **a representation of a number less than $x$ uses only elements less than $x$.**

**Lemma.** If $x\in S$ and $x>3m$, then the next element of $S$ after $x$ is $2x$.

*(i) No $y\in S$ with $x<y<2x$.* Suppose there is one.
* If $y>x+m$: $y-x\in(m,x)$ has $k$ representations, all using elements $<x$; adding $x$ gives $k$ representations of $y$ not containing $y$. Together with $\{y\}$, $y$ has at least $k+1$ representations — contradiction.
* If $y\le x+m$: let $z=2x-1$. Then $z-x=x-1\in(m,x)$ has $k$ representations using elements $<x$; adding $x$ gives $k$ representations of $z$ containing $x$ but not $y$. Also $z-y\ge x-1-m>m$ and $z-y<x$, so $z-y$ has a representation using elements $<x$; adding $y$ gives a representation of $z$ containing $y$ but not $x$. So $z>m$ has at least $k+1$ representations — contradiction.

*(ii) $2x\in S$.* Suppose not. Representations of $2x$ containing $x$ correspond to representations of $x$ not containing $x$; since $x$ has $k$ representations, one of them being $\{x\}$, there are exactly $k-1$. So $2x$ has a representation $R$ not containing $x$. By (i) and $2x\notin S$, all elements of $R$ are $<x$. If $R$ contains some $u<x-m$, then $y=2x-u\in(x+m,2x)$ has the representation $R\setminus\{u\}$ (without $x$), and also, as $y-x=x-u\in(m,x)$ has $k$ representations by elements $<x$, $k$ representations containing $x$: in total $k+1$ — contradiction. So all elements of $R$ lie in $[x-m,x)$. Two of them sum to less than $2x$, and three or more sum to at least $3(x-m)>2x$ (as $x>3m$) — contradiction. $\square$

**Structure of $S$.** Fix $x\in S$ with $x>3m$. By the lemma (applied to $x,2x,4x,\dots$, all $>3m$), $S=T\cup U$ with $T=S\cap[1,x)$ finite and $U=\{x,2x,4x,\dots\}$. Sums of distinct elements of $U$ are exactly the non-negative multiples of $x$, each in exactly one way (binary).

**Counting.** Let $y>\max(m,s(T))$. A representation of $y$ is a set $T'\subseteq T$ together with a representation of $y-s(T')>0$ by elements of $U$; this exists (uniquely) iff $s(T')\equiv y\pmod x$. So
$$k=\#\{T'\subseteq T:\ s(T')\equiv y\pmod x\}.$$
Letting $y$ run through $x$ consecutive values, every residue class mod $x$ contains the sums of exactly $k$ subsets of $T$. Hence $2^{|T|}=kx$, so $k$ divides a power of $2$ and is itself a power of $2$.

**Answer:** $k=2^a$, $a=0,1,2,\dots$ ∎

apmo-2020-04.title: Pigeonhole for degree 1, greedy construction otherwise
apmo-2020-04.body:
**Degree $1$ works.** Let $P(x)=cx+d$, $c\ne0$. Its values are exactly the integers $\equiv d\pmod{|c|}$; write $c'=|c|$. Let $s_i=a_1+\dots+a_i$ ($s_0=0$). Infinitely many terms satisfy $a_e\equiv d\pmod{c'}$; pick $c'+1$ such indices $e>1$. For each, $s_e\equiv s_{e-1}+d$, and $s_{e-1}$ takes at most $c'$ residues, so there are two such indices $e<e'$ with $s_{e-1}\equiv s_{e'-1}\pmod{c'}$. Then
$$a_e+a_{e+1}+\dots+a_{e'}=s_{e'}-s_{e-1}\equiv s_{e'-1}+d-s_{e-1}\equiv d\pmod{c'},$$
a sum of at least two consecutive terms that is a value of $P$.

**Lemma.** If $\deg P\ne1$, then for all positive integers $A,B,C$ there is an integer $y$ with $|y|>C$ such that no value $P(k)$, $k\in\mathbb{Z}$, lies in $[y-A,y+B]$.

*Proof.* If $P$ is constant or of even degree, $P$ is bounded on one side, say $P(k)\ge-V$ for all $k$ (or $\le V$); take $y=-(V+B+C+1)$ (or $y=V+A+C+1$). If $\deg P=n\ge3$ is odd, assume the leading coefficient is positive (else replace $P(x)$ by $P(-x)$, which has the same values). Then $P(k+1)-P(k)$ is a polynomial of even degree $n-1\ge2$ with positive leading coefficient, so there is $K$ such that for $k\ge K$: $P(k+1)-P(k)>A+B+1$ and $P(k)>0$, and for $k\le-K$: $P(k)<0$. Let $V=\max_{|k|<K}|P(k)|$ and take $k_0\ge K$ with $P(k_0)>V+C$. Put $y=P(k_0)+A+1$. The interval $[y-A,y+B]=[P(k_0)+1,P(k_0)+A+B+1]$ lies strictly between $P(k_0)$ and $P(k_0+1)$; it contains no $P(k)$ with $k\ge K$ ($P$ increases there), none with $k\le-K$ (negative), and none with $|k|<K$ (at most $V$). $\square$

**Degree $\ne1$ fails.** We build a permutation $a_1,a_2,\dots$ of $\mathbb{Z}$ in which no sum of at least two consecutive terms is a value of $P$, adding two terms per stage. Suppose $a_1,\dots,a_i$ (distinct) are built with that property. Let $m$ be an unused integer of smallest absolute value. We set $a_{i+2}=m$ and choose $a_{i+1}=y$. The new sums of at least two consecutive terms are
$$y+(a_l+\dots+a_i),\quad y+m+(a_l+\dots+a_i)\ (1\le l\le i),\quad y+m,$$
all of the form $y+f$ with $f$ in a finite set $F$ fixed before choosing $y$. Pick $A,B$ with $F\subseteq[-A,B]$ and $C$ larger than $|m|$ and all $|a_l|$; the lemma gives $y$ with $|y|>C$ such that all new sums avoid the values of $P$. Then $y$ is unused and $y\ne m$.

Every sum of at least two consecutive terms is checked at the stage where its last term is added. Every integer $t$ appears: there are only $2|t|+1$ integers of absolute value $\le|t|$, so after finitely many stages $t$ is the unused integer of smallest absolute value and is placed. Each integer appears once. So this sequence defeats $P$.

**Answer:** all $P(x)=cx+d$ with integers $c\ne0$ and $d$. ∎

apmo-2020-05.title: A potential function and a recursive construction
apmo-2020-05.body:
**Lower bound.** Each move adds $1$ stone to the first bucket and $\gcd(a,b)\ge1$ to the second, so $t\ge s$.

**Upper bound.** Each move increases the sum $p$ of the numbers by $1$, so $s=p-n$. Write the numbers in a row $a_1,\dots,a_n$; when $a_i$ and $a_j$ ($i<j$) are erased, put $a_i+a_j$ in position $j$ and $1$ in position $i$. Let
$$q=\sum_{k=1}^n(k-1)a_k .$$
Since all $a_k\ge1$, $q=\sum(k-1)(a_k-1)+\sum(k-1)\le(n-1)(p-n)+\frac{n(n-1)}2=(n-1)s+\frac{n(n-1)}2$.

In a move on positions $i<j$, $t$ increases by $\gcd(a_i,a_j)\le a_i$, while $q$ increases by
$$(j-1)a_i-(i-1)(a_i-1)\ge ia_i-(i-1)(a_i-1)=a_i+i-1\ge a_i .$$
So $q-t$ never decreases. As all numbers start equal to $1$, we may label them so that the first move uses position $n$. Right after it, $q=\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}(k-1)+2(n-1)=\frac{(n-1)(n+2)}2$ and $t=1$. Therefore at any later time
$$t\le q+1-\frac{(n-1)(n+2)}2\le(n-1)s+\frac{n(n-1)}2-\frac{(n-1)(n+2)}2+1=(n-1)s-(n-2)<(n-1)s .$$
So $\frac ts$ is a rational number in $[1,n-1)$.

**Construction.** After one move, $\frac ts=1$. Now let $a\ge2$.

*Claim.* With $N\ge2$ numbers equal to $1$, one can reach the board ($N-1$ ones and the number $a^{N-1}$) with $s=a^{N-1}-1$ and $t=a^{N-2}(a-1)(N-1)$.

For $N=2$, every move is $(1,x)\to(1,x+1)$ with $\gcd=1$; after $a-1$ moves the board is $1,a$ with $s=t=a-1$. For $N\ge3$, let $\mathcal A$ be the procedure for $N-1$ numbers. Apply $\mathcal A$ to $N-1$ of the ones (getting $a^{N-2}$); then repeat $a-1$ times: apply $\mathcal A$ to the $N-1$ ones, producing another $a^{N-2}$, and combine it with the big number $c\,a^{N-2}$ (gcd $a^{N-2}$). The big number ends as $a\cdot a^{N-2}=a^{N-1}$; $s=p-N=a^{N-1}-1$; and
$$t=a\cdot a^{N-3}(a-1)(N-2)+(a-1)a^{N-2}=a^{N-2}(a-1)(N-1).$$

Use the claim with $N=n$, then make $b$ further moves combining a $1$ with the big number (gcd $1$). Then
$$\frac ts=\frac{T+b}{S+b},\qquad T=a^{n-2}(a-1)(n-1),\ S=a^{n-1}-1 .$$
Given a rational $\frac uv\in(1,n-1)$ with positive integers $u>v$, we need $v(T+b)=u(S+b)$, i.e.
$$b=\frac{vT-uS}{u-v}.$$
Choose $a\equiv1\pmod{u-v}$; then $T\equiv S\equiv0\pmod{u-v}$, so $b$ is an integer. Moreover
$$vT-uS>v\,a^{n-2}(a-1)(n-1)-u\,a^{n-1}=a^{n-2}\bigl(a\,(v(n-1)-u)-v(n-1)\bigr),$$
which is positive for large $a$ because $v(n-1)-u>0$. So $b$ is a positive integer and $\frac ts=\frac uv$.

**Answer:** every rational number in $[1,n-1)$. ∎
